prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence on how import competition and technological change shape employment, wages and adjustment in local labour markets

statement.case_for: My laureate set is unchanged from round 1: Autor, Dorn and Hanson under B036. I narrowed the citation after the exchange, and that is the only change. I dropped 'wage inequality' and 'labour demand' as headline claims. The local-labour-market evidence speaks most directly to employment, wages and adjustment in exposed places. It does not establish the economy-wide wage structure, which is the territory of the skill-premium and task literatures. My case rests on three criteria applied to every field. First, the question is first-order: who bears the adjustment costs of trade and technology. Second, the identification is transparent, with local exposure measures and instrumented import competition that others could and did contest. In the 2024 presentation speech I said a prize-worthy contribution should provide solid causal evidence, and this body of work offers that more convincingly than the cross-country evidence behind my own opening first choice, B047. Third, there has been about a decade of replication and hostile re-examination. The central finding, large and persistent local adjustment costs, has survived in qualified form. Attribution is the tightest of the shortlisted items: the foundational papers are jointly authored by the three named people. The chair notes that the convergence on B036 came partly from members revising their ballots, and I was one of them. I do not count that convergence as evidence of merit. I tested my own move against the rival cases from Enflo (B034), Krusell (B018) and Friberg (B020), and the narrower citation, not the head count, is why I stay with B036.
statement.case_against: The ballot entry bundles two strands, the task and skill-bias literature and the trade-shock literature. The trio credits only the second in full, leaving Katz and the task lineage unrecognised. Part of that lineage involves Acemoglu, who was recognised in 2024, and Levy and Murnane, who are outside the credited set. The magnitude and long-run persistence of the China-shock effects, the shift-share exposure measures and the trade-versus-automation attribution are still contested. My own 2024 speech put weight on causal credibility. That standard cuts both ways, because it requires me to be precise about what the evidence identifies, namely local adjustment and not aggregate welfare. There is also thematic proximity to the 2021 labour prize, the 2023 prize and the 2024 technology-and-institutions prize. A member who sees these as leaving no room for another labour-and-technology award could reasonably reject my configuration.

responses.point: Andersson moved from Autor, Hanson and Katz to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He argued that Autor's work spans both strands, which gives the citation a coherent centre. He also argued that the citation should rest on the empirical exposure evidence and not on the theory of tasks, to avoid the Acemoglu overlap.
responses.response: I agree with his anchoring and I take it further. He keeps 'wage inequality' in the citation, and I now think it overreaches, because the local-labour-market designs identify employment and wage effects in exposed places and not the economy-wide wage structure. Autor links the strands, but that is a reason to name technological change as a source of exposure and not to write a citation that claims the task framework. I have therefore cut 'wage inequality' from my wording. I accept his conclusion that Katz and the task lineage go uncredited. I do not think the citation can honestly cover them with three names.

responses.point: Boppart supports B036 for its clean three-name attribution. He asked me whether B047 could be framed so that it does not depend on contested cross-country constitutional results. He also noted that the 2024 prize makes the thematic overlap with B047 harder to dismiss.
responses.response: I think it can be framed that way only in part. The formal theory of electoral rules, accountability and state capacity is a distinct contribution, and Besley's state-capacity work with Persson is separate from the constitutions strand. A citation anchored there would not need the cross-country estimates. But such a citation would then credit a theoretical programme whose empirical support is the contested part. That is exactly the causal-evidence standard I used in the 2024 speech, and I cannot waive it for a field that is close to my own. This is why B047 is an alternative and not my lead. I agree with his point about overlap with 2024, which I weigh as thematic proximity and not as disqualifying. If the Committee wanted a political-economics prize, I would want a three-person award, because dropping Besley would damage the attribution.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B034 (Helpman, Melitz). She argues that its maturity is not in doubt, that it has no dispute about magnitudes and no recent adjacent prize in the same lineage, and that Redding should be left out because his work builds on the framework.
responses.response: This is the strongest rival case outside my own field, and I take the maturity point seriously. I ranked B034 sixth in my opening and added Redding. Her argument about Redding persuades me that a two-person core is cleaner, and I would not press a third name. I do not accept that B034 escapes the objection I put to B036. She and Strömberg agree that the welfare gains depend on model structure, and the priority questions involving Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are unresolved on the evidence supplied. B036's persistence debate is about the size of effects, while B034's open questions concern priority and structure-dependence of the headline claims. These are different problems, and I do not find one clearly lighter than the other. A specific finding would change my view: if the shift-share and persistence critiques turned out to undermine the central claim of lasting local adjustment costs, and not just its size, I would move to B047 or B003 and would take B034 seriously.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson moved from Katz to Dorn, partly because Katz's skill-premium work lies close to the 2023 prize. She disagrees that the strands cannot be bundled, and she says the overlap with the Goldin and Acemoglu prizes should be tested when the citation is drafted, not assumed.
responses.response: She is right that this should be tested in drafting, and I withdraw my earlier phrasing that the strands are hard to bundle. The accurate version is that they should not be credited as one theory. I cannot state precisely what the task strand adds beyond what the 2023 and 2024 prizes covered. The chair asked for this and I do not have a clean answer. That is my reason for leaving it out of the credit and not for including it with a weak case. Her suggestion to name the shared object, labour-market adjustment to technology and trade, is how I rewrote the citation. I would keep the technology half in the wording only as a source of exposure. I also accept that this leaves a real attribution cost for Katz.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B020 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn). He ranks B036 seventh because the debate over identification, persistence and magnitude makes him doubt maturity. He says he would not oppose B036.
responses.response: His maturity worry is the right question and I answer it in two parts. The finding that import exposure lowered local employment and wages in the most exposed places has held across the main critiques and across countries, so I treat it as established. The long-run aggregate magnitudes are not settled, and the citation should not claim them. On B020 I agree that structural demand estimation is mature and very widely used, but I give weight to the fact that it is a methods contribution, as he concedes, with open attribution questions around Bresnahan and Pakes's dynamic work. I do not think these are lighter than B036's problems. I appreciate that he says he would not oppose B036, and I would say the same about B020 on scientific grounds.

uncertainties: Whether the persistence and shift-share critiques, reviewed directly, support a lasting discovery of local adjustment costs, or reduce it to a contested estimate.

Whether leaving out Katz and the task lineage, including originators outside the credited set such as Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane, is an acceptable attribution cost for a trade-and-technology citation.
How much room the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes leave for another award on labour, technology and trade.
Whether B034 would be stronger than B036 if the priority questions around Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum could be settled, which I cannot do from the evidence supplied.
I rely on my own reading of the literature, not on independent verification of attributions, and my disciplinary distance from economics is a limit as well as a source of independence.
statement.conflict_note: No collaboration or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson is apparent from my supplied profile. I disclose field proximity to B047 (political science, institutions and democratisation), which I had ranked first in the opening and now hold as an alternative. I gave the 2024 presentation speech on a thematically adjacent prize. My profile lists a co-authored paper with a 'Persson' (with Rothstein), and the supplied profile does not identify that co-author. I cannot say whether it is Torsten Persson, who is credited on B047, so I record it as possibly relevant to an alternative and not to my preferred part. I am a Stockholm University colleague of Hassler, Krusell and Boppart, in a different department. Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated.
